paper.title: The effects of unemployment on fertility
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement is printed and no Statistics Denmark project number is given. …

registers.name_in_paper: Danish administrative panel data collected by Statistics Denmark around the personal identification number

registers.role: treatment (monthly unemployment indicator) and first-stage outcome

registers.name_in_paper: the registers [that] provide reliable yearly information on all private sector Danish firms
data on births, stillbirths and registered miscarriages, including the length of the mother's pregnancy (described as hospital records)

linkages: All residents of Denmark have a unique personal number; the data for each individual can be linked to his or her partners (married or cohabiting) and children.
Workers are linked to uniquely identified private-sector firms, which allows firm closures to be dated.
Children's birthdays and the length of the mother's pregnancy are linked to the parent, which allows the month of conception to be computed.

sample.universe: All residents of Denmark born in 1966 (N = 87,333), followed monthly in the registers from age 16 (1982) until age 40 (2006).
selection_rules: Follow each individual monthly from age 16 (1982) to age 40 (2006).
First sample: all person-month observations until the individual conceives his or her first child; individuals who do not conceive before age 40 are right-censored at age 40.
Second sample: all person-month observations from the conception of the first child to the conception of the second child; contains only individuals with one child; right-censored at age 40.
Restrict both samples to individuals employed in private-sector firms with more than four employees; public firms are excluded because their closures cannot be identified.
Keep only the months in which the individual was employed in such a firm, so months in the public sector or in small firms are dropped even for included individuals.
sample.n_observations: First sample: 6,501,531 person-month observations. Second sample: 1,784,356 person-month observations. (The estimation samples reported in the tables are 4,093,613 men and 2,192,288 women person-months for first births, and 1,085,999 men and 698,357 women person-months for second births.)
sample.n_individuals: First sample: 74,556 individuals (40,923 men and 33,633 women). Second sample: 41,432 individuals (22,079 men and 19,353 women).

construction_notes: The month of conception is computed from the child's birthday and the length of the mother's pregnancy, so pre-term deliveries are timed correctly.

Conceptions include those ending in live birth, stillbirth and registered miscarriage; abortions and intentions to conceive are not observed. Before 1997 a stillbirth was a non-living birth after the 27th week of pregnancy; from 1997 the cut-off is the 20th week.

A firm is treated as closed when it disappears from the yearly register of private firms, except when it (1) changes address with the same owner and industry, (2) changes address with the same owner and employees, (3) changes owner but keeps the same employees and address, or (4) changes owner but keeps the same employees and industry. 'Same employees' means at least 30 percent of employees continue from one year to the next.
The month of closure is the month in which the unemployment rate among the firm's employees increased by 50 percent or more relative to the preceding month.
The average number of employees of the sample firms that closed is 222 (standard deviation 645.2).
Age is recoded into 24 binary variables, one for each year between age 16 and age 40, giving a flexible piecewise-constant duration dependence.
Previous unemployment is the share of months observed in the data until the current month in which the individual has been unemployed.
All partner information is set to zero in months in which the individual has no partner.
For unemployed individuals the last known industry is assigned; industry dummies are coded monthly but vary only yearly in the registers.
Models are linear probability models applied to data set up as for a discrete-time duration model (Jenkins 1995), estimated with ivreg in Stata; standard errors are clustered on the individual.
No separate 'out of labour force' category is used; those months are counted in the employed reference category.
Average observation length before first birth is about 191 months, with a minimum of 24 months and a maximum (censoring) of 300 months.

claims.statement: Being unemployed in a given month lowers the monthly probability of conceiving a first child among Danish men of the 1966 cohort (reduced-form OLS linear probability model, without controls).

register_source.value: unemployment benefit registers (no Statistics Denmark register code given)

definition.value: A monthly indicator of whether the individual was unemployed in a given month, constructed from unemployment benefit registers; the indicator does not distinguish between insured and uninsured unemployed, and the reference category is 'employed' (which also absorbs the very few months out of the labour force).

timing.value: Measured in the same month as the conception indicator

outcome.label: First birth (monthly indicator of conception of the first child)

definition.value: A monthly indicator of the individual's timing of the first-child conception, which may result in a miscarriage, live birth or stillbirth. The month of conception is computed from the child's birthday and the measured duration of the pregnancy; the indicator equals one in the month of conception and the individual is right-censored at age 40 if no conception occurs.

timing.value: Monthly, over the person-months of the first-birth sample

units.value: change in the monthly probability (hazard) of conception (linear probability model coefficient), for an unemployed person-month relative to an employed one

estimand.target_population: All person-months of men in the first-birth sample
estimand.time_horizon: Contemporaneous within the month: the monthly unemployment (or firm-closure) indicator and the monthly conception indicator refer to the same month
estimand.formal_query: E[Y | unemployed = 1, X] - E[Y | unemployed = 0, X], Y = the monthly probability of conceiving a first child

population.description: Danish 1966 birth cohort: person-month observations from age 16 (1982) until the conception of the first child, right-censored at age 40 (2006); only months in which the individual was employed in a private-sector firm with more than four employees. Men only.
population.selection: Person-months enter only when the individual was employed in a private-sector firm with more than four employees; public-sector months, months in firms with four or fewer employees and months out of employment are dropped. The second-birth sample is further conditional on having conceived a first child.

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation is used: this is the reduced-form discrete-time duration model common in the literature, in which the monthly unemployment indicator enters directly. The authors state these models support no causal claim and serve as a benchmark for the 2SLS specifications.

key_assumptions.assumption: No causal interpretation is claimed: the reduced-form models describe the association between the monthly unemployment indicator and conception, conditional on the observed covariates and fixed effects.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors state the reduced-form models do not allow causal claims and serve mainly as a benchmark for the 2SLS models.

key_assumptions.assumption: For a causal reading, unemployment would have to be as good as randomly assigned given the controls and fixed effects; the paper argues it is not, which motivates the instrument.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Motivation in the introduction and Section 3.2; the authors argue a series of interlinked events and preferences determine both fertility and the likelihood of being unemployed.

rhs: Unobserved determinants of the conception decision

implies_edges.from: Unobserved determinants of the conception decision

key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a data restriction; no test of the resulting selection is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: The linear probability model is an adequate linear approximation of the discrete-time hazard, so the coefficients can be read as hazard rates.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in the table notes to Tables 2 and 3 and in Section 3.2; not tested.

register_source.value: unemployment benefit registers (no Statistics Denmark register code given)

population.description: Danish 1966 birth cohort: person-month observations from age 16 (1982) until the conception of the first child, right-censored at age 40 (2006); only months in which the individual was employed in a private-sector firm with more than four employees. Men only.
population.selection: Person-months enter only when the individual was employed in a private-sector firm with more than four employees; public-sector months, months in firms with four or fewer employees and months out of employment are dropped. identification.source_of_variation: Unexpected closures of private-sector Danish firms with more than four employees, 1982-2006, used as an exogenous source of individual unemployment; 11,778 of the 74,556 individuals in the first sample (15.8 percent) and 2992 of the 41,432 in the second sample (7.2 percent) experienced at least one closure.
identification.instrument: Firm closure (a monthly dummy for the closure of the private-sector firm employing the individual)

population.description: Danish 1966 birth cohort: person-month observations from age 16 (1982) until the conception of the first child, right-censored at age 40 (2006); only months in which the individual was employed in a private-sector firm with more than four employees. Men only.
population.selection: Person-months enter only when the individual was employed in a private-sector firm with more than four employees; public-sector months, months in firms with four or fewer employees and months out of employment are dropped. The second-birth sample is further conditional on having conceived a first child.

identification.source_of_variation: Unexpected closures of private-sector Danish firms with more than four employees, 1982-2006, used as an exogenous source of individual unemployment; 11,778 of the 74,556 individuals in the first sample (15.8 percent) and 2992 of the 41,432 in the second sample (7.2 percent) experienced at least one closure.
identification.instrument: Firm closure (a monthly dummy for the closure of the private-sector firm employing the individual)

key_assumptions.assumption: Exclusion restriction / independence: the instrument affects fertility only through unemployment, so experiencing a firm closure has no direct effect on the conception decision.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table A9 (p. 14) compares the fertility outcomes of individuals who did and did not become unemployed after experiencing a firm closure; the observed difference is read as evidence that the unemployment, not the closure itself, drives the results.

implies_edges.to: First birth (monthly indicator of conception of the first child)

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: employees do not foresee the closure and leave the firm before it is recorded (the 'early-leavers' problem).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table A10 (p. 15) re-estimates the IV models with the treatment group expanded to include individuals who left the firm in the six months before the closure.

implies_edges.to: First birth (monthly indicator of conception of the first child)

key_assumptions.assumption: Monotonicity: the instrument always moves individuals in the same direction, so there are no defiers who become employed because of the closure.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued verbally only; the authors concede they cannot rule the mechanism out entirely but claim the model complies with monotonicity.

register_source.value: unemployment benefit registers (no Statistics Denmark register code given)

claims.statement: Being unemployed in a given month lowers the monthly probability of conceiving a first child among Danish men of the 1966 cohort (2SLS instrumenting unemployment with firm closures, with the full set of controls, lagged instrument (2 months)).

register_source.value: unemployment benefit registers (no Statistics Denmark register code given)

definition.value: A monthly indicator of whether the individual was unemployed in a given month, constructed from unemployment benefit registers; the indicator does not distinguish between insured and uninsured unemployed, and the reference category is 'employed' (which also absorbs the very few months out of the labour force).

timing.value: Measured in the same month as the conception indicator

outcome.label: First birth (monthly indicator of conception of the first child)

definition.value: A monthly indicator of the individual's timing of the first-child conception, which may result in a miscarriage, live birth or stillbirth. The month of conception is computed from the child's birthday and the measured duration of the pregnancy; the indicator equals one in the month of conception and the individual is right-censored at age 40 if no conception occurs.

timing.value: Monthly, over the person-months of the first-birth sample

units.value: change in the monthly probability (hazard) of conception (linear probability model coefficient), for an unemployed person-month relative to an employed one

estimand.target_population: Compliers: individuals who would have been kept on had the firm survived but who are not skilled enough to find another job once it closes.
estimand.compliers: Of the 11,778 individuals in the first sample and the 2992 in the second sample who experienced a firm closure, only 10.1 per cent and 11.9 per cent respectively became unemployed as a result; these are the compliers whose behaviour the LATE describes.
estimand.time_horizon: Contemporaneous within the month: unemployment and conception are measured in the same month, with the instrument lagged by 2 months
estimand.formal_query: E[Y | do(unemployed = 1)] - E[Y | do(unemployed = 0)] for the compliers, Y = the monthly probability of conceiving a first child

population.description: Danish 1966 birth cohort: person-month observations from age 16 (1982) until the conception of the first child, right-censored at age 40 (2006); only months in which the individual was employed in a private-sector firm with more than four employees. Men only.
population.selection: Person-months enter only when the individual was employed in a private-sector firm with more than four employees; public-sector months, months in firms with four or fewer employees and months out of employment are dropped. The second-birth sample is further conditional on having conceived a first child.

identification.source_of_variation: Unexpected closures of private-sector Danish firms with more than four employees, 1982-2006, used as an exogenous source of individual unemployment; 11,778 of the 74,556 individuals in the first sample (15.8 percent) and 2992 of the 41,432 in the second sample (7.2 percent) experienced at least one closure.
identification.instrument: Firm closure (a monthly dummy for the closure of the private-sector firm employing the individual)

key_assumptions.assumption: Exclusion restriction / independence: the instrument affects fertility only through unemployment, so experiencing a firm closure has no direct effect on the conception decision.

value.equation_number: 2 (second stage; Eq. 1 is the first stage)
value.as_printed:
unemployment_it = α_it + δ1 x_it + θ firm closure_it + r_it   (1)
fertility outcome_it = α2 + δ2 x_it + β unemployment̂_it + u_it   (2)
value.normalisation: Unemployment is measured relative to the reference category 'employed'; education dummies relative to elementary school; married/cohabiting relative to single.
value.link_function: identity (linear probability model; no logit link)

value.claimed_domain: Individuals who became unemployed specifically because of a firm closure – the compliers whose behaviour the local average treatment effect describes.
boundary_conditions: The authors add that, because of the generosity and gender-egalitarian nature of the Danish welfare state, effects found in Danish data probably represent lower-bound estimates of a comparable effect in other countries (p. 4).

anchor_quote.text: Although the sizes vary, the coefficients have similar signs for “first birth” across all models.

claims.statement: Being unemployed in a given month raises the monthly probability of conceiving a first child among Danish women of the 1966 cohort (2SLS instrumenting unemployment with firm closures, with the full set of controls, lagged instrument and lagged unemployment (1 month)).

register_source.value: unemployment benefit registers (no Statistics Denmark register code given)

definition.value: A monthly indicator of whether the individual was unemployed in a given month, constructed from unemployment benefit registers; the indicator does not distinguish between insured and uninsured unemployed, and the reference category is 'employed' (which also absorbs the very few months out of the labour force).

timing.value: Measured 1 month(s) before the conception indicator (lagged unemployment)

outcome.label: First birth (monthly indicator of conception of the first child)

definition.value: A monthly indicator of the individual's timing of the first-child conception, which may result in a miscarriage, live birth or stillbirth. The month of conception is computed from the child's birthday and the measured duration of the pregnancy; the indicator equals one in the month of conception and the individual is right-censored at age 40 if no conception occurs.

timing.value: Monthly, over the person-months of the first-birth sample

units.value: change in the monthly probability (hazard) of conception (linear probability model coefficient), for an unemployed person-month relative to an employed one

estimand.target_population: Compliers: individuals who would have been kept on had the firm survived but who are not skilled enough to find another job once it closes.
estimand.compliers: Of the 11,778 individuals in the first sample and the 2992 in the second sample who experienced a firm closure, only 10.1 per cent and 11.9 per cent respectively became unemployed as a result; these are the compliers whose behaviour the LATE describes.
estimand.time_horizon: Contemporaneous within the month, with both the instrument and the unemployment indicator lagged by 1 month
estimand.formal_query: E[Y | do(unemployed = 1)] - E[Y | do(unemployed = 0)] for the compliers, Y = the monthly probability of conceiving a first child

population.description: Danish 1966 birth cohort: person-month observations from age 16 (1982) until the conception of the first child, right-censored at age 40 (2006); only months in which the individual was employed in a private-sector firm with more than four employees. Women only.
population.selection: Person-months enter only when the individual was employed in a private-sector firm with more than four employees; public-sector months, months in firms with four or fewer employees and months out of employment are dropped. The second-birth sample is further conditional on having conceived a first child.

identification.source_of_variation: Unexpected closures of private-sector Danish firms with more than four employees, 1982-2006, used as an exogenous source of individual unemployment; 11,778 of the 74,556 individuals in the first sample (15.8 percent) and 2992 of the 41,432 in the second sample (7.2 percent) experienced at least one closure.
identification.instrument: Firm closure (a monthly dummy for the closure of the private-sector firm employing the individual)

key_assumptions.assumption: Exclusion restriction / independence: the instrument affects fertility only through unemployment, so experiencing a firm closure has no direct effect on the conception decision.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table A9 (p. 14) compares the fertility outcomes of individuals who did and did not become unemployed after experiencing a firm closure; the observed difference is read as evidence that the unemployment, not the closure itself, drives the results.

implies_edges.to: First birth (monthly indicator of conception of the first child)

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: employees do not foresee the closure and leave the firm before it is recorded (the 'early-leavers' problem).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table A10 (p. 15) re-estimates the IV models with the treatment group expanded to include individuals who left the firm in the six months before the closure.

implies_edges.to: First birth (monthly indicator of conception of the first child)

key_assumptions.assumption: Monotonicity: the instrument always moves individuals in the same direction, so there are no defiers who become employed because of the closure.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued verbally only; the authors concede they cannot rule the mechanism out entirely but claim the model complies with monotonicity.

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument relevance: firm closures raise the probability of unemployment.
key_assumptions.supported_by: F-test of the excluded instrument = 31.77***, printed with this estimate.

formal.as_written: unemployment_it = α_it + δ1 x_it + θ firm closure_it + r_it   (1)

key_assumptions.assumption: The unemployment that results from the firm closure is not correlated with employee characteristics that also drive fertility.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from the institutional setting (firms with more than four employees, so a single worker's fertility cannot bring the firm down) and from the industry and region fixed effects that absorb the non-random distribution of closures.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection: only person-months in which the individual is employed in a private-sector firm with more than four employees enter the estimation sample.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a data restriction; the authors argue it eliminates the feedback of an individual's fertility on the firm's survival. No test of the resulting selection is reported.

implies_edges.from: Employment in a private-sector firm with more than four employees

threats_discussed: Anticipation of the closure by early-leavers who depart before the closure is recorded
Defiers: a closure may improve reemployment chances, violating monotonicity
A direct effect of the firm closure on fertility other than through unemployment
Endogeneity of the partner's characteristics
Endogeneity of previous unemployment
Individuals exposed to more than one firm closure
Reverse causality from fertility to firm survival in very small firms
robustness_checks: Excluding partner variables (Table A3)
Excluding months spent in singlehood (Table A4)
Lagging the instrument, and the instrument together with unemployment, by one to three months (Tables A5 and A6)
Excluding previous unemployment from the controls (Table A7)
Dropping individuals with more than one firm closure (Table A8)
Re-estimating the OLS models on the firm-closure-only subsample (Table A9)
Expanding the treatment group to include early-leavers (Table A10)
Re-estimating with ivprobit (footnote 15, p. 5; results described as similar but not reported)
unresolved_confounders: Defiers cannot be ruled out entirely: a local job centre may make an exceptional effort for workers hit by a large closure, and a closure-related job loss may protect workers from the stigma of unemployment (p. 7).
The authors cannot distinguish the income-loss effect of unemployment from the uncertainty it induces (p. 12).
The treatment sample of individuals who became unemployed after their firm closed may be a heterogeneous group (p. 12).

claims.statement: Being unemployed in a given month lowers the monthly probability of conceiving a first child among Danish men of the 1966 cohort (2SLS instrumenting unemployment with firm closures, with the full set of controls, lagged instrument and lagged unemployment (3 months)).

register_source.value: unemployment benefit registers (no Statistics Denmark register code given)

definition.value: A monthly indicator of whether the individual was unemployed in a given month, constructed from unemployment benefit registers; the indicator does not distinguish between insured and uninsured unemployed, and the reference category is 'employed' (which also absorbs the very few months out of the labour force).

timing.value: Measured 3 month(s) before the conception indicator (lagged unemployment)

outcome.label: First birth (monthly indicator of conception of the first child)

definition.value: A monthly indicator of the individual's timing of the first-child conception, which may result in a miscarriage, live birth or stillbirth. The month of conception is computed from the child's birthday and the measured duration of the pregnancy; the indicator equals one in the month of conception and the individual is right-censored at age 40 if no conception occurs.

timing.value: Monthly, over the person-months of the first-birth sample

units.value: change in the monthly probability (hazard) of conception (linear probability model coefficient), for an unemployed person-month relative to an employed one

estimand.target_population: Compliers: individuals who would have been kept on had the firm survived but who are not skilled enough to find another job once it closes.
estimand.compliers: Of the 11,778 individuals in the first sample and the 2992 in the second sample who experienced a firm closure, only 10.1 per cent and 11.9 per cent respectively became unemployed as a result; these are the compliers whose behaviour the LATE describes.
estimand.time_horizon: Contemporaneous within the month, with both the instrument and the unemployment indicator lagged by 3 months
estimand.formal_query: E[Y | do(unemployed = 1)] - E[Y | do(unemployed = 0)] for the compliers, Y = the monthly probability of conceiving a first child

population.description: Danish 1966 birth cohort: person-month observations from age 16 (1982) until the conception of the first child, right-censored at age 40 (2006); only months in which the individual was employed in a private-sector firm with more than four employees. Men only.
population.selection: Person-months enter only when the individual was employed in a private-sector firm with more than four employees; public-sector months, months in firms with four or fewer employees and months out of employment are dropped. The second-birth sample is further conditional on having conceived a first child.

identification.source_of_variation: Unexpected closures of private-sector Danish firms with more than four employees, 1982-2006, used as an exogenous source of individual unemployment; 11,778 of the 74,556 individuals in the first sample (15.8 percent) and 2992 of the 41,432 in the second sample (7.2 percent) experienced at least one closure.
identification.instrument: Firm closure (a monthly dummy for the closure of the private-sector firm employing the individual)

key_assumptions.assumption: Exclusion restriction / independence: the instrument affects fertility only through unemployment, so experiencing a firm closure has no direct effect on the conception decision.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table A9 (p. 14) compares the fertility outcomes of individuals who did and did not become unemployed after experiencing a firm closure; the observed difference is read as evidence that the unemployment, not the closure itself, drives the results.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued verbally only; the authors concede they cannot rule the mechanism out entirely but claim the model complies with monotonicity.

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument relevance: firm closures raise the probability of unemployment.

claims.statement: Being unemployed in a given month does not measurably change the monthly probability of conceiving a second child among Danish women of the 1966 cohort (2SLS instrumenting unemployment with firm closures, with the full set of controls, lagged instrument (2 months)).

register_source.value: unemployment benefit registers (no Statistics Denmark register code given)

definition.value: A monthly indicator of whether the individual was unemployed in a given month, constructed from unemployment benefit registers; the indicator does not distinguish between insured and uninsured unemployed, and the reference category is 'employed' (which also absorbs the very few months out of the labour force).

timing.value: Measured in the same month as the conception indicator

outcome.label: Second birth (monthly indicator of conception of the second child)

definition.value: A monthly indicator of the timing of the second conception, defined analogously to the first-conception indicator and measured over person-months running from the conception of the first child to the conception of the second child; right-censored at age 40.

timing.value: Monthly, over the person-months of the second-birth sample

units.value: change in the monthly probability (hazard) of conception (linear probability model coefficient), for an unemployed person-month relative to an employed one

estimand.target_population: Compliers: individuals who would have been kept on had the firm survived but who are not skilled enough to find another job once it closes.
estimand.compliers: Of the 11,778 individuals in the first sample and the 2992 in the second sample who experienced a firm closure, only 10.1 per cent and 11.9 per cent respectively became unemployed as a result; these are the compliers whose behaviour the LATE describes.
estimand.time_horizon: Contemporaneous within the month: unemployment and conception are measured in the same month, with the instrument lagged by 2 months
estimand.formal_query: E[Y | do(unemployed = 1)] - E[Y | do(unemployed = 0)] for the compliers, Y = the monthly probability of conceiving a second child

population.description: Danish 1966 birth cohort: person-month observations from the conception of the first child to the conception of the second child (individuals with one child only), right-censored at age 40 (2006); only months in which the individual was employed in a private-sector firm with more than four employees. Women only.
population.selection: Person-months enter only when the individual was employed in a private-sector firm with more than four employees; public-sector months, months in firms with four or fewer employees and months out of employment are dropped. The second-birth sample is further conditional on having conceived a first child.

identification.source_of_variation: Unexpected closures of private-sector Danish firms with more than four employees, 1982-2006, used as an exogenous source of individual unemployment; 11,778 of the 74,556 individuals in the first sample (15.8 percent) and 2992 of the 41,432 in the second sample (7.2 percent) experienced at least one closure.
identification.instrument: Firm closure (a monthly dummy for the closure of the private-sector firm employing the individual)

key_assumptions.assumption: Exclusion restriction / independence: the instrument affects fertility only through unemployment, so experiencing a firm closure has no direct effect on the conception decision.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table A9 (p. 14) compares the fertility outcomes of individuals who did and did not become unemployed after experiencing a firm closure; the observed difference is read as evidence that the unemployment, not the closure itself, drives the results.

implies_edges.to: Second birth (monthly indicator of conception of the second child)

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: employees do not foresee the closure and leave the firm before it is recorded (the 'early-leavers' problem).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table A10 (p. 15) re-estimates the IV models with the treatment group expanded to include individuals who left the firm in the six months before the closure.

implies_edges.to: Second birth (monthly indicator of conception of the second child)

key_assumptions.assumption: Monotonicity: the instrument always moves individuals in the same direction, so there are no defiers who become employed because of the closure.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued verbally only; the authors concede they cannot rule the mechanism out entirely but claim the model complies with monotonicity.

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument relevance: firm closures raise the probability of unemployment.

register_source.value: unemployment benefit registers (no Statistics Denmark register code given)

definition.value: A monthly indicator of whether the individual was unemployed in a given month, constructed from unemployment benefit registers; the indicator does not distinguish between insured and uninsured unemployed, and the reference category is 'employed' (which also absorbs the very few months out of the labour force).

timing.value: Measured 2 month(s) before the conception indicator (lagged unemployment)

outcome.label: Second birth (monthly indicator of conception of the second child)

definition.value: A monthly indicator of the timing of the second conception, defined analogously to the first-conception indicator and measured over person-months running from the conception of the first child to the conception of the second child; right-censored at age 40.

timing.value: Monthly, over the person-months of the second-birth sample

units.value: change in the monthly probability (hazard) of conception (linear probability model coefficient), for an unemployed person-month relative to an employed one

estimand.target_population: Compliers: individuals who would have been kept on had the firm survived but who are not skilled enough to find another job once it closes.
estimand.compliers: Of the 11,778 individuals in the first sample and the 2992 in the second sample who experienced a firm closure, only 10.1 per cent and 11.9 per cent respectively became unemployed as a result; these are the compliers whose behaviour the LATE describes.
estimand.time_horizon: Contemporaneous within the month, with both the instrument and the unemployment indicator lagged by 2 months
estimand.formal_query: E[Y | do(unemployed = 1)] - E[Y | do(unemployed = 0)] for the compliers, Y = the monthly probability of conceiving a second child

population.description: Danish 1966 birth cohort: person-month observations from the conception of the first child to the conception of the second child (individuals with one child only), right-censored at age 40 (2006); only months in which the individual was employed in a private-sector firm with more than four employees. Men only.
population.selection: Person-months enter only when the individual was employed in a private-sector firm with more than four employees; public-sector months, months in firms with four or fewer employees and months out of employment are dropped. The second-birth sample is further conditional on having conceived a first child.

identification.source_of_variation: Unexpected closures of private-sector Danish firms with more than four employees, 1982-2006, used as an exogenous source of individual unemployment; 11,778 of the 74,556 individuals in the first sample (15.8 percent) and 2992 of the 41,432 in the second sample (7.2 percent) experienced at least one closure.
identification.instrument: Firm closure (a monthly dummy for the closure of the private-sector firm employing the individual)

key_assumptions.assumption: Exclusion restriction / independence: the instrument affects fertility only through unemployment, so experiencing a firm closure has no direct effect on the conception decision.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table A9 (p. 14) compares the fertility outcomes of individuals who did and did not become unemployed after experiencing a firm closure; the observed difference is read as evidence that the unemployment, not the closure itself, drives the results.

implies_edges.to: Second birth (monthly indicator of conception of the second child)

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: employees do not foresee the closure and leave the firm before it is recorded (the 'early-leavers' problem).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table A10 (p. 15) re-estimates the IV models with the treatment group expanded to include individuals who left the firm in the six months before the closure.

implies_edges.to: Second birth (monthly indicator of conception of the second child)

key_assumptions.assumption: Monotonicity: the instrument always moves individuals in the same direction, so there are no defiers who become employed because of the closure.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued verbally only; the authors concede they cannot rule the mechanism out entirely but claim the model complies with monotonicity.

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument relevance: firm closures raise the probability of unemployment.
key_assumptions.supported_by: F-test of the excluded instrument = 35.06***, printed with this estimate.

formal.as_written: unemployment_it = α_it + δ1 x_it + θ firm closure_it + r_it   (1)

key_assumptions.assumption: The unemployment that results from the firm closure is not correlated with employee characteristics that also drive fertility.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from the institutional setting (firms with more than four employees, so a single worker's fertility cannot bring the firm down) and from the industry and region fixed effects that absorb the non-random distribution of closures.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection: only person-months in which the individual is employed in a private-sector firm with more than four employees enter the estimation sample.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a data restriction; the authors argue it eliminates the feedback of an individual's fertility on the firm's survival. No test of the resulting selection is reported.

implies_edges.from: Employment in a private-sector firm with more than four employees

Excluding months spent in singlehood (Table A4)

estimand.target_population: Compliers: individuals who would have been kept on had the firm survived but who are not skilled enough to find another job once it closes.
estimand.compliers: Of the 11,778 individuals in the first sample and the 2992 in the second sample who experienced a firm closure, only 10.1 per cent and 11.9 per cent respectively became unemployed as a result; these are the compliers whose behaviour the LATE describes.
estimand.time_horizon: Contemporaneous within the month, with both the instrument and the unemployment indicator lagged by 3 months
estimand.formal_query: E[Y | do(unemployed = 1)] - E[Y | do(unemployed = 0)] for the compliers, Y = the monthly probability of conceiving a second child

population.description: Danish 1966 birth cohort: person-month observations from the conception of the first child to the conception of the second child (individuals with one child only), right-censored at age 40 (2006); only months in which the individual was employed in a private-sector firm with more than four employees. Women only.
population.selection: Person-months enter only when the individual was employed in a private-sector firm with more than four employees; public-sector months, months in firms with four or fewer employees and months out of employment are dropped. The second-birth sample is further conditional on having conceived a first child.

identification.source_of_variation: Unexpected closures of private-sector Danish firms with more than four employees, 1982-2006, used as an exogenous source of individual unemployment; 11,778 of the 74,556 individuals in the first sample (15.8 percent) and 2992 of the 41,432 in the second sample (7.2 percent) experienced at least one closure.

identification.source_of_variation: Unexpected closures of private-sector Danish firms with more than four employees, 1982-2006, used as an exogenous source of individual unemployment; 11,778 of the 74,556 individuals in the first sample (15.8 percent) and 2992 of the 41,432 in the second sample (7.2 percent) experienced at least one closure.

register_source.value: unemployment benefit registers (no Statistics Denmark register code given)

definition.value: A monthly indicator of whether the individual was unemployed in a given month, constructed from unemployment benefit registers; the indicator does not distinguish between insured and uninsured unemployed, and the reference category is 'employed' (which also absorbs the very few months out of the labour force).

timing.value: Measured in the same month as the conception indicator

outcome.label: First birth (monthly indicator of conception of the first child)

definition.value: A monthly indicator of the individual's timing of the first-child conception, which may result in a miscarriage, live birth or stillbirth. estimand.target_population: Compliers: individuals who would have been kept on had the firm survived but who are not skilled enough to find another job once it closes.
estimand.compliers: Of the 11,778 individuals in the first sample and the 2992 in the second sample who experienced a firm closure, only 10.1 per cent and 11.9 per cent respectively became unemployed as a result; these are the compliers whose behaviour the LATE describes.
estimand.time_horizon: Contemporaneous within the month: the monthly unemployment (or firm-closure) indicator and the monthly conception indicator refer to the same month
estimand.formal_query: E[Y | do(unemployed = 1)] - E[Y | do(unemployed = 0)] for the compliers, Y = the monthly probability of conceiving a first child

population.description: Danish 1966 birth cohort: person-month observations from age 16 (1982) until the conception of the first child, right-censored at age 40 (2006); only months in which the individual was employed in a private-sector firm with more than four employees. Women only.
population.selection: Person-months enter only when the individual was employed in a private-sector firm with more than four employees; public-sector months, months in firms with four or fewer employees and months out of employment are dropped. identification.source_of_variation: Unexpected closures of private-sector Danish firms with more than four employees, 1982-2006, used as an exogenous source of individual unemployment; 11,778 of the 74,556 individuals in the first sample (15.8 percent) and 2992 of the 41,432 in the second sample (7.2 percent) experienced at least one closure.
identification.instrument: Firm closure (a monthly dummy for the closure of the private-sector firm employing the individual)

key_assumptions.assumption: Exclusion restriction / independence: the instrument affects fertility only through unemployment, so experiencing a firm closure has no direct effect on the conception decision.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table A9 (p. 14) compares the fertility outcomes of individuals who did and did not become unemployed after experiencing a firm closure; the observed difference is read as evidence that the unemployment, not the closure itself, drives the results.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection: only person-months in which the individual is employed in a private-sector firm with more than four employees enter the estimation sample.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a data restriction; the authors argue it eliminates the feedback of an individual's fertility on the firm's survival. No test of the resulting selection is reported.

implies_edges.from: Employment in a private-sector firm with more than four employees

threats_discussed: Anticipation of the closure by early-leavers who depart before the closure is recorded
Defiers: a closure may improve reemployment chances, violating monotonicity
A direct effect of the firm closure on fertility other than through unemployment
Endogeneity of the partner's characteristics
Endogeneity of previous unemployment
Individuals exposed to more than one firm closure
Reverse causality from fertility to firm survival in very small firms
robustness_checks: Excluding partner variables (Table A3)
Excluding months spent in singlehood (Table A4)
Lagging the instrument, and the instrument together with unemployment, by one to three months (Tables A5 and A6)
Excluding previous unemployment from the controls (Table A7)
Dropping individuals with more than one firm closure (Table A8)
Re-estimating the OLS models on the firm-closure-only subsample (Table A9)
Expanding the treatment group to include early-leavers (Table A10)
Re-estimating with ivprobit (footnote 15, p. 5; results described as similar but not reported)
unresolved_confounders: Defiers cannot be ruled out entirely: a local job centre may make an exceptional effort for workers hit by a large closure, and a closure-related job loss may protect workers from the stigma of unemployment (p. 7).
The authors cannot distinguish the income-loss effect of unemployment from the uncertainty it induces (p. 12).
The treatment sample of individuals who became unemployed after their firm closed may be a heterogeneous group (p. 12).

heterogeneity.dimension: sex (men vs women), estimated in separate models
heterogeneity.finding: The paper reports men and women separately throughout. In the 2SLS models on first births the effect is positive and significant for women (0.105 without controls, 0.143 with controls) and negative and insignificant for men once controls are included (Table 4, p. 9); on second births neither sex shows a significant effect (Table 5, p. 10).

heterogeneity.dimension: birth parity (first vs second birth)
heterogeneity.finding: The paper tests the prediction that the substitution effect is stronger for first than for second or higher-order births and reports no significant effect of unemployment on second births for either sex.
